Sierra History · The Mail Route Over the Snow

The Snowshoe Thompson Story

For twenty winters, one Norwegian immigrant was the only reliable link between California and the settlements snowed in beyond the Sierra — ninety miles of blizzard and cornice, crossed alone on ten-foot skis, with the United States mail on his back. He was never paid a cent.

1856 – 1876Placerville → Genoa90 miles, on skis

Lake Tahoe in winter, from the high country Thompson crossed twice a month for twenty years. His route passed south of the lake, over Johnson and Luther passes and down through Hope Valley.

In the winter of 1855–56, the settlers of Carson Valley — in what was then Utah Territory, now Nevada — were, in the words of the day, “lost to the world.” Snow closed the Sierra Nevada passes from roughly November to May. Stagecoaches stopped. Pack trains stopped. The mail contractors who were supposed to cross on woven Canadian snowshoes had failed, and one had simply disappeared. For months at a time, the valley's only news of the outside world was rumor.

Then a 28-year-old Norwegian walked into the Placerville post office, on the California side of the mountains, and offered to carry the mail over the top — in midwinter, on his back, using a kind of snow travel nobody in California had ever seen. The postmaster made him come back five mornings in a row to prove he meant it. He did. And then he kept coming back, twice a month, for twenty years.

His name was John Albert Thompson. The Sierra knew him by a better one.

Chapter One

A boy from Telemark

He was born Jon Torsteinson Rue on April 30, 1827, on the Luraas-Rue farm in Tinn, in Telemark, Norway — steep, snowbound country where skis were not sport but transportation, as ordinary as shoes. Telemark is, not coincidentally, the region modern skiing traces its turns to. A Telemark boy learned to glide almost as soon as he learned to walk, and young Jon learned on long wooden skis with a single pole, held out in front with both hands for balance.

His father died when Jon was ten. In 1837 his mother, Gro, brought the family to America, settling first in the Fox River Norwegian settlement in Illinois, then moving on as the frontier pulled west. The boy took an American name — John Albert Thompson, after his stepfather — and grew into a big man: about six feet tall and 180 pounds, blond, blue-eyed, and built for hauling.

Gold pulled him the rest of the way. In 1851, at 24, Thompson drove a herd of milk cows to California and settled at Placerville — Hangtown — in the heart of the Mother Lode. He tried mining at Coon Hollow and the Kelsey Diggings, and like most miners found more work than gold in it. He took up a ranch on Putah Creek instead. But he had grown up in mountains, and the white wall of the Sierra, visible all winter from the foothills, seems to have worked on him. When he heard the valley on the far side of it was cut off and crying out for mail, he recognized a job that was, quite literally, made for the skills of his childhood.

There was a personal edge to it, too. Thompson knew what it was to wait on letters that came too late: word of the illness that killed his mother had reached him long after the fact. The mail mattered to him in a way it might not have to another man.

Chapter Two

“People lost to the world; Uncle Sam needs a mail carrier”

In late 1855 the Sacramento Union carried the appeal that made him famous: the Placerville postmaster needed someone to carry the overland mail ninety miles east, up and over the Sierra to Mormon Station — the settlement that would become Genoa, Nevada — in the dead of winter. The previous contractor had vanished. Conventional snowshoes, the broad woven kind, were hopeless in Sierra powder: a man sank, floundered, and made a few miles a day at best.

Thompson's answer was to build the tool of his boyhood from memory. Working from a green oak plank, he carved a pair of skis roughly ten feet long and a few inches wide, with upturned tips — and weighed them, famously, at about 25 pounds the pair. Californians had never seen anything like them. The papers called them “Norwegian snowshoes” or “Norwegian skates,” and the name that stuck to the man himself came straight from that misunderstanding: they weren't snowshoes at all, but to everyone who watched him leave, he was Snowshoe Thompson.

He practiced in the high country above Placerville, then, in January 1856, shouldered the mail sack in front of a gathered crowd and set off east into the storm wall. Skeptics expected to organize a search party. Instead, he was back in about six days — having covered 180 miles round trip, delivered the mail to a stunned Carson Valley, and brought theirs back. The eastward climb took him three days; the long glide home, two.

“He flew down the mountainside. He did not ride astride his pole or drag it to one side… but held it horizontally before him after the manner of a tightrope walker… in the manner that a soaring eagle dips its wings.”
Dan De Quille, Territorial Enterprise, on Thompson's style

That single-pole technique — both hands on one long staff, held out level like a tightrope walker's bar — became his signature. You can still recognize him by it in every statue: no other skier on the frontier moved that way.

The route: Placerville to Genoa

Thompson followed Johnson's Cutoff and the old emigrant road — roughly today's U.S. 50 over Echo Summit, then south over Luther Pass and down through Hope Valley, country Dave's Highway 88 runs through today. Tap each stop to walk it with him.

Chapter Three

Twenty winters on the route

For twenty winters — 1856 to 1876 — Thompson made the crossing at least twice a month, in all weathers. Sierra snowpacks run twenty to fifty feet deep on the passes; winds on the crest can top 80 miles an hour. He crossed in blizzards that buried every landmark, navigating, he said, by the shape of the peaks and the set of familiar trees, the way his Viking ancestors had steered by an unmarked sea. He carried no compass, no blanket, and no gun. His provisions were beef jerky and biscuits; his rest, when he rested, was sometimes a hole dug in the snow or a night spent stamping in a circle to keep from freezing.

And the mail was only the beginning of the load. His sack ran sixty to ninety pounds of letters, and past a hundred when the valley's shopping list went in:

  • Letters & newspapersThe valley's whole connection to family, news, and the outside world for months at a time.
  • MedicineCarried both ways — including, famously, the chloroform that saved a man's life (Chapter Four).
  • A printing press, in piecesType and newsprint for Nevada's first newspaper, the Territorial Enterprise — first issued December 18, 1858.
  • Ore samplesIncluding the strange blue rock of 1859 that turned out to be the Comstock Lode (Chapter Five).
  • Small merciesFiddle strings for the local musician, needles and a lamp chimney for a widow's winter sewing, books, tools, pots and pans.
  • PeopleMore than once, a lost or exhausted traveler rode out on the back of his skis, arms around him.

He was not only a mailman. In 1859 he and Judge John Childs ran a winter sleigh line for passengers and express over the passes — arguably the first scheduled winter transport service across the Sierra. Later he also carried mail on the Big Tree Route, between Genoa and Murphys Camp by way of the Calaveras big trees country. And in the summers, when the snow released him, he farmed.

The legend grew taller than the man, as legends do. Newspapers credited him with downhill runs near sixty miles an hour and jumps past a hundred feet — Paul Bunyan numbers, best read as the measure of how he looked to people who had never seen anyone ski at all. The verifiable record needs no embroidery: in 2001, three fit young men retraced his route on modern lightweight cross-country gear. It took them six days. Thompson routinely did it in two or three — carrying a hundred pounds, on 25-pound oak planks he had carved himself.

Chapter Four

The rescues

The mail runs would have been enough. What made Thompson a hero rather than a curiosity was what he did when the route crossed somebody dying.

Just before Christmas 1856, on one of his first winter's crossings, he stopped at a cabin in Lake Valley, south of Lake Tahoe, that he sometimes used for rest — and found prospector James Sisson inside. Sisson had been snowbound there for twelve days. The furniture had been burned for fuel; there was no fire and nothing to eat but raw flour. Both his feet were frozen.

Thompson chopped wood, built a fire, and left Sisson with fuel and what comfort he could. Then he skied on to Genoa, and on Christmas Day talked five men into going back with him — first carving them skis of their own and teaching them to use them, and rigging a sled to haul Sisson out. They got the prospector down to Genoa alive, but the doctor's verdict was grim: the frozen feet would have to come off, and there was no chloroform in the valley to operate with.

So Thompson went back over the Sierra. He crossed to Placerville — no chloroform there either — and pushed on fifty more miles to Sacramento, where he got the bottle. Then he turned around and crossed the mountains again, alone, through winter, carrying the anesthetic back to Genoa. The operation succeeded. Sisson lived. By the usual telling, Thompson had covered some 400 miles in ten days — the better part of it on skis, in December, much of it in service of a stranger he had found by chance in a cabin.

It was not a one-off. Across twenty winters he pulled lost travelers out of storms, guided the disoriented, and carried the stranded on his skis — among them, by report, a young C. J. “Lucky” Baldwin, who would go on to make a fortune in California. Thompson never charged for any of it. Rescuing people was simply part of what the route meant to him: he was the only thing moving out there, so anything that went wrong in that white country was, by default, his responsibility.

Chapter Five

The blue rock

In 1859, miners in the Washoe diggings, on the eastern slope, kept cursing a heavy blue-black rock that clogged their gold rockers and dragged down the value of their dust. Somebody finally thought to have it assayed — and the man asked to carry the sample over the Sierra to Sacramento was Thompson.

The blue rock was silver. Spectacularly rich silver — the first ore taken from what became the Comstock Lode, the greatest silver strike in American history. The Territorial Enterprise later credited Thompson's ski-borne assay run with accelerating both the Comstock discovery and Nevada statehood itself: in a snowbound winter, the news — and the proof — moved at exactly the speed of one man on skis.

The Comstock changed his route's whole economy. Virginia City exploded out of the strike, and Thompson extended his carrying to serve it year-round. But the same boom built the thing that ended his era: in 1868–69 the Central Pacific drove the transcontinental railroad over the Sierra at Donner Pass, and mail that had depended on one man's legs for a decade began moving by locomotive, in any weather, on a schedule. Thompson kept carrying packages and express for private parties for a time. The mountains, though, no longer needed him the way they had.

The era in one view

Thompson's twenty winters span the whole arc of the Sierra's transformation: he started when Carson Valley was a Mormon trading-post outpost in Utah Territory, cut off half the year — and he finished in a Nevada that had been a state for a decade, stitched to California by rail and telegraph. He was, as Dan De Quille put it, “the pioneer of the pack train, the stage coach, and the locomotive” — the man who held the route open until the machines arrived.

Chapter Six

The man who was never paid

Here is the fact that still stops readers cold: in twenty years of carrying the United States mail, Thompson was never paid for it. He worked as a subcontractor's subcontractor in an era of loose contracts and looser bookkeeping; the paperwork that would have entitled him to his wages never existed, or never reached him. He petitioned. He pressed his claim for years. In 1872 he traveled all the way to Washington, D.C., to argue it in person — and came home empty-handed.

He kept crossing anyway. That is the part the valley remembered: the pay was a grievance, but it was never the reason. He carried the mail, by every account, for the look on people's faces when he glided into a snowed-in settlement with letters from home.

The private man behind the legend was substantial in his own right. In 1860 he homesteaded a 160-acre ranch in Diamond Valley, in Alpine County just south of Genoa — wheat, oats, hay, and potatoes, and irrigation work his neighbors long credited him with helping design. From 1868 to 1872 he sat on the Alpine County Board of Supervisors, and in 1871 he was a delegate to the Republican state convention in Sacramento.

In 1866 he married Agnes Singleton, an English immigrant living in Genoa. Their only child, Arthur Thomas, was born February 11, 1867. The boy was eleven when diphtheria took him in 1878; he is buried beside his father.

Thompson himself died on May 15, 1876, at his Diamond Valley ranch — appendicitis that developed into pneumonia, at 49 years old. Travel Nevada records his last words, spoken to his son: “Always be a good boy, Arthur. Mind your mother and be good to her.” His funeral at the Genoa courthouse was grand and crowded, and he was laid to rest in the Genoa Cemetery, a half-mile north of the town he had kept connected to the world for twenty winters.

His life, in brief

  1. Apr 30, 1827

    Born in Telemark

    Jon Torsteinson Rue is born on a mountainside farm in Tinn, Telemark, Norway — ski country, where he learns to travel on long wooden skis as a small boy.

  2. 1837

    Emigration

    His father dead, ten-year-old Jon sails for America with his mother, settling among Norwegian immigrants in Illinois.

  3. 1851

    California

    Now John A. Thompson, he drives a herd of milk cows west and settles at Placerville, mining at Coon Hollow and Kelsey Diggings, then ranching on Putah Creek.

  4. Jan 1856

    The first crossing

    Answering the Sacramento Union's appeal, he carves ten-foot oak skis and makes the 180-mile Placerville–Genoa round trip in about six days. A legend — and a mail route — is born.

  5. Dec 1856

    The Sisson rescue

    Finds James Sisson frozen and starving in a Lake Valley cabin; organizes his rescue, then crosses the Sierra twice more to fetch chloroform from Sacramento. Sisson lives.

  6. Dec 1858

    A newspaper on his back

    Carries type and newsprint over the range for Nevada's first newspaper, the Territorial Enterprise, first issued December 18, 1858.

  7. 1859

    The blue rock

    Carries the first Comstock ore sample to Sacramento for assay. It is rich silver; the Comstock rush — and Nevada's future — follows.

  8. 1860–66

    Diamond Valley

    Homesteads 160 acres in Diamond Valley, Alpine County (1860). Marries Agnes Singleton of Genoa (1866); son Arthur is born in 1867.

  9. 1868–72

    Supervisor; the railroad

    Serves on the Alpine County Board of Supervisors. The transcontinental railroad's completion over Donner Pass ends the era that made his crossings essential.

  10. 1872

    Washington

    Travels to Washington, D.C., to press his claim for twenty years of unpaid mail service. He is turned away.

  11. May 15, 1876

    Death at 49

    Dies of appendicitis and pneumonia at his Diamond Valley ranch. Buried in Genoa Cemetery after a funeral at the Genoa courthouse.

  12. 1970

    Hall of Fame

    Inducted posthumously into the U.S. National Ski Hall of Fame — the “father of California skiing.” Nevada lawmakers were still urging a commemorative postage stamp in his honor as recently as 2025.

Epilogue

In his tracks today

The eastern half of Thompson's world is Highway 88 country — a short drive from Fiddletown. His Diamond Valley ranch sat just south of Woodfords, under the same peaks you cross at Carson Pass; Hope Valley, which he traversed on every trip, is the broad meadow valley the highway winds through today. When Highway 88 is buried in a big winter storm and the plows are running day and night to keep one lane open, it's worth remembering that for twenty years the “road” over this range was one man, and he never once failed to get through.

  • Mormon Station State Historic Park — Genoa, NVHis statue, the reconstructed 1851 trading post, and the eastern terminus of the route, all in one small park in Nevada's oldest town.
  • Genoa Courthouse Museum & Genoa CemeteryThe courthouse where his funeral was held holds a Snowshoe Thompson exhibit; his grave, beside Arthur's, is a half-mile north of town.
  • Placerville Main StreetThe Gold Rush town he departed from — historic buildings, the bell tower, and the post office site where he reported five mornings running to prove he meant it.
  • The route itself: U.S. 50 → Luther Pass → Hope Valley → Hwy 88Drive his crossing in an hour or two: Echo Summit, Meyers, Luther Pass, Hope Valley, Woodfords, and Diamond Valley below — best in winter, when it looks the way he saw it.
  • Carson Pass & Highway 88A Thompson monument stands along Highway 88, on one of his later routes; the pass country shows the scale of the Sierra winter he crossed alone.
  • Boreal Mountain, Donner SummitAnother of his monuments stands at the ski area on Donner Pass — fittingly, at a lift-served mountain, honoring the man who brought skiing to California.

Norway remembers him, too: a memorial stands in Austbygde, in his home district of Telemark, and skiers there honor him with a memorial run every Palm Sunday — the boy from Rue farm, still setting the pace, a century and a half on.

“He was the father of all the race of snow-shoers in the Sierra Nevada Mountains; and in those mountains he was the pioneer of the pack train, the stage coach, and the locomotive.”
Dan De Quille, Overland Monthly, 1886
